meta.icd10: ICD-10 diagnosis titles extracted from birgermoell/icd10-clinical-notes (en/ro/ru).
meta.harvard_en: English term list from harvard_medical_dictionary.json already in this repo.
meta.hospital_ops: Meeting/hospital workflow terms, curated for Medpark minutes. Short forms and phrases from the team's listening notes (asr-llm/data/pattern.png).
meta.harvard_icu: Harvard Health dictionary + ICU list. RO/RU from Wikidata labels where a medical entity exists, else machine translation checked by back-translation (back_ok). Spot-check before relying on it.

aligned.en: Malignant neoplasm of bronchus and lung
aligned.ro: Neoplasm malign al bronhiei și plămânului
Infecții acute ale căilor respiratorii superioare

aligned.en: patient in bed N (bed number, not the word four)
sent up to another floor or department

aligned.def_en: Pus that collects in a pocket of swollen, red tissue. Often occurs on the surface of the skin.
Abbreviation for angiotensin-converting enzyme, an enzyme that converts the inactive form of the protein angiotensin (angiotensin I) to its active form—angiotensin II.

aligned.ro: inhibitor al enzimei de conversie a angiotensinei
aligned.def_en: Abbreviation of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, a drug used to treat high blood pressure and congestive heart failure.
The main breakdown product of alcohol metabolism; accumulation of it in the bloodstream may produce flushing (a feeling of heat in the face or chest) and vomiting.
A common, over-the-counter drug used to reduce fever and relieve mild to moderate pain, but which does not reduce redness or swelling (inflammation).
A neurotransmitter (a chemical messenger that sends signals between brain cells) that plays roles in attention, learning, and memory.
An inflammatory disease resulting from excess sebum production, follicle plugging, and increased bacterial production.

Usually abbreviated as AIDS. This is the most advanced stage of infection with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), which can severely weaken the immune system. People with AIDS get many infections, often from diseases that don’t affect people with healthy immune systems.
The term given to the brain's absorption of new information to begin creating a memory.
A shoulder joint that connects the clavicle to the scapula.
One of the proteins that allows cells to move and muscles to contract.
Using the thumb or fingers to apply pressure to particular spots, or pressure points, on the body in order to relieve pain.
A treatment based on Chinese medicine. Thin needles are inserted into the skin at specific points on the body. This therapy is used to treat pain and various health problems and to reduce stress.
The ability of the body to learn to fight specific infections after being exposed to the germs that cause them.
An energy-storing molecule that is found in all human cells. Usually abbreviated as ATP.
A band of scar-like tissue that forms between two surfaces inside the body, connecting tissues or organs which are not normally connected.
Fat-filled tissue.
Glands that sit on top of each kidney and secrete stress hormones.
Stress hormone that puts the body on high alert. Changes include faster heartbeat, more rapid breathing, greater energy, and higher blood pressure. Also called epinephrine.
Excessive swallowing of air.
A rare disease in which a person can’t recognize objects, shapes, or people. Often due to a brain or neurological condition.
Fear and avoidance of public places and open spaces.
abbreviation for acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, the most advanced stage of infection with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).
A group of inherited conditions that typically appear as a reduction or absence of melanin pigments in the skin, hair, and eyes.
A protein made by the liver. Abnormal levels of this substance may indicate liver or kidney disease.
High amounts of albumin (a protein made by the liver) in the urine, possibly indicating kidney dysfunction.
Continuing consumption of alcohol despite alcohol-related social or interpersonal problems.
A liver enzyme that metabolizes alcohol into a substance called acetaldehyde, which is toxic. Sometimes referred to as ADH.

Another term for alcohol dependence: A chronic, progressive disease characterized by excessive and often compulsive drinking, impaired control over drinking, use of alcohol despite adverse consequences, and withdrawal symptoms when alcohol use is discontinued. Also known as alcoholism.
A hormone secreted by the adrenal glands that helps regulate blood pressure by controlling sodium and potassium levels in the body.
Another term for the gastrointestinal, or digestive, tract.
One of two or more versions of a gene. Different alleles produce variations in inherited characteristics, such as eye color.
A substance such as fur, pollen, or dust that produces an allergic reaction.

A seasonal or year-round allergic condition marked by sneezing, runny nose, and congestion. The most common type of allergy, it is caused by an IgE-mediated immune response to inhaled airborne allergens.
An immune system reaction (for example, rash, fever, sneezing, or headaches) to something that is normally harmless.
Pain resulting from something not normally painful, such as a light touch.
Tiny air sacs in the lung. They are where oxygen enters and carbon dioxide leaves the bloodstream.
A progressive brain disease that causes memory loss, impaired thinking, and personality changes.
Abbreviation for age-related macular degeneration, a potentially blinding condition that destroys sharp central vision.
Unusual memory loss or forgetfulness.
Part of the brain involved in memory and emotion.
An enzyme secreted by the pancreas that breaks starch into sugar.
The last inch of the large intestine, leading to the anal opening.
Absence of pain.
A drug or other substance such as aspirin, acetaminophen, or morphine that is used to relieve pain.
A severe allergic reaction, causing symptoms spanning from itching and swelling to trouble breathing, convulsions, shock, and coma.
Any of a group of male sex hormones, including testosterone, that controls male characteristics such as beard growth.
Having a lower than normal amount of red blood cells or hemoglobin (an oxygen-carrying protein inside red blood cells), leading to low energy, weakness, and other symptoms.
A bulge or swelling on a portion of a blood vessel, due to weakness in the wall of that vessel.
A test that shows how blood moves through the blood vessels and heart. It uses x-rays and the injection of a fluid called a contrast agent that can be seen on the x-rays.
A procedure used to open blocked or narrowed arteries, most commonly by inserting a thin tube, or catheter, into the affected artery and inflating a balloon.
A protein that raises blood pressure by narrowing blood vessels and causing the kidneys to store more sodium and water.
An enzyme that converts the inactive form of the protein angiotensin (angiotensin I) to its active form—angiotensin II. Usually abbreviated as ACE.
A disease that leads to swelling between the disks of the spine and in the joints where the pelvis and spine meet. Causes back pain and stiffness and can limit movement.
An eating disorder in which a person has an intense fear of gaining weight and severely limits calories to the point of near starvation.
A protein made by the immune system to protect the body from harmful substances, called antigens.
A substance that helps prevent blood from clotting.

Drugs that diminish the blood's ability to clot. Anticoagulants are sometimes called blood thinners even though they do not thin the blood. Commonly used anticoagulant drugs include heparin and warfarin.
Drugs used to treat seizures.
A psychiatric drug used to treat mood disorders, such as depression.
A drug that prevents nausea and vomiting.
Any substance that the body sees as harmful or foreign, causing the immune system to form antibodies in defense.
Medications that treat allergies and reduce symptoms such as sneezing and itching by blocking histamine, the substance in the body which causes these symptoms.
Substances that protect the body from molecules that damage cells (free radicals); examples include beta carotene, vitamin C, vitamin A, and vitamin E.
A drug used to treat schizophrenia and other severe mental health disorders; relieves symptoms such as delusions and hallucinations.
Substances used on wounds to prevent or treat infection; they kill or slow the growth of disease-causing organisms, such as bacteria, on the surface of the body.
The large artery emerging from the heart's left ventricle that distributes blood to the body.
A valve on the left side of the heart that acts as a one-way gate, opening to allow blood to leave the left ventricle and closing to prevent blood from leaking back into that ventricle.
Difficulty speaking or comprehending language; a common occurrence after a stroke affecting the left hemisphere of the brain, where language is processed.
A temporary pause in breathing during sleep that can be very brief or can last so long that the amount of oxygen in the blood drops dangerously low.
Proteins that combine with cholesterol and triglyceride to form lipoproteins.
A process of programmed cell death in which redundant or flawed cells destroy themselves.
Clear fluid that fills the front part of the eye.
A virus transmitted by mosquitoes or other member of the arthropod phylum.
An abnormal heart rhythm caused by a disturbance in the heart’s electrical system.

A term encompassing a variety of conditions in which artery walls thicken and become less flexible. Sometimes called hardening of the arteries. Arteriosclerosis occurs when cholesterol-rich plaque forms on the inner lining of arteries (atherosclerosis), when artery walls become calcified, or when high blood pressure thickens the muscular wall of arteries.
A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart and to various parts of the body.
A condition in which joints are inflamed, causing pain, stiffness, swelling, and sometimes loss of movement.
Joint disease or disorder.
A life-threatening lack of oxygen due to drowning, choking, or an obstruction of the airways.
A drug that relieves pain, fever, and swelling, and inhibits the formation of blood clots.

aligned.ru: учреждение по оказанию помощи в проживании
aligned.def_en: Live-in facilities for adults who need help with certain things, but do not need round-the-clock care. They provide residents with supervision and certain services, such as meals, transportation, or help with dressing, grooming, and other daily activities.
Blurry vision caused by an irregular curve in the cornea of the eye.
Being unable to control movement; symptoms include shaking and an unsteady walk.
An abnormal build-up of fatty plaque inside an artery.
The buildup of fatty deposits (plaque) in the walls of arteries, causing narrowing and reduced blood flow; the disease responsible for most heart attacks and many strokes.
A mixture of fats, cholesterol, and other tissue that builds up on artery walls.
Another name for the topmost vertebra of the neck, which lies just beneath the skull. Also called C-1.
A long-term skin condition, most common in babies and children, in which areas of the skin are dry, itchy, red, and may crack. Also known as eczema.
A seasonal or year-round allergy marked by sneezing, runny nose, and congestion.
Abbreviation for adenosine triphosphate, an energy-storing molecule that is found in all human cells.
A disorder in which the two upper chambers of the heart beat fast and erratically. Because blood isn’t pumped out of these chambers fully, it may pool and form clots that could lead to a stroke.
Wasting away of an organ or tissue due to undernourishment, disease, or aging.
A health professional who assesses hearing and fits hearing aids.
A disease in which the immune system mistakenly identifies healthy tissues and organs as threats and responds by attacking and destroying them.
The part of the nervous system that controls involuntary actions, such as blood pressure or breathing. It also plays an important role in the fight or flight response to danger.
Surgically opening and examining a body after death to see if any diseases are present and to determine the cause of death.
The long, slender extension of a nerve cell that conducts electrical impulses away from the nerve's cell body and on to nearby nerves.
White blood cells that come from bone marrow, and produce antibodies to fight off disease.
Tiny single-celled organisms. Some bacteria cause disease, although most are harmless.
A procedure to open clogged heart arteries. A surgeon inserts and inflates a tiny balloon. It widens the blocked artery then expands a small wire mesh tube to keep the artery open.
The most common skin cancer. Basal cell carcinoma doesn’t spread to internal organs.
The artery that supplies blood to the cerebellum, the brainstem, and the back of the brain.
A noncancerous enlargement of the prostate gland that obstructs the flow of urine. Often called BPH.
Anti-anxiety medications that work by helping to maintain levels of the neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) in the brain.
The period of grief and mourning after a death.
A nervous system or heart disorder caused by lack of the vitamin thiamine (B1).
A richly colored compound (red, yellow, or orange) found in many plants, fruits, and vegetables that the body can convert into vitamin A.
A thick, yellow-green fluid produced by the liver that aids in digestion.
Fatty substances made by the gallbladder that aid in digestion.
The ability of both eyes to focus on an object and form a single visual image.
How quickly and completely the body can absorb and use a nutrient.
An treatment that helps people learn to gain control over normally unconscious body functions, such as breathing and heart rates.
A distinctive biological indicator of an event, process, or condition.
The removal of a small piece of tissue from the body for examination under a microscope.
Medications, including alendronate and etidronate, used to prevent and treat osteoporosis by slowing the breakdown of bone.
An episode of temporary memory loss resulting from the ingestion of alcohol or other drugs.
A small pocket of fluid that develops between the upper layers of skin; often caused by friction or burns.
A measure of the amount of alcohol in the blood.
The force blood exerts against the walls of the arteries. Optimal blood pressure is less than 120/80 mm Hg.
Hollow tubes that transport blood throughout the body; includes arteries, veins, and capillaries.

Abbreviation for body-mass index, a measure of body fat estimated from a person’s height and weight. A healthy BMI is defined as 18.5 to 24.9. BMI = weight (in kilograms) divided by height (in meters) squared. Using English units, multiply weight in pounds by 703, then divide the result by height in inches, and divide that result by height in inches.

A measure of body fat estimated from a person’s height and weight. A healthy BMI is defined as 18.5 to 24.9. BMI = weight (in kilograms) divided by height (in meters) squared. Using English units, multiply weight in pounds by 703, then divide the result by height in inches, and divide that result by height in inches.
Brand name for a drug made of botulinum toxin type A that is injected into muscles and weakens them to ease the appearance of wrinkles.
Abbreviation for benign prostatic hyperplasia, a noncancerous enlargement of the prostate gland that obstructs the flow of urine.
A network of nerves that are rooted at the cervical spine and provide sensation and movement to the shoulder and arm.
A slow heart rate, usually below 60 beats per minute.
The part of the brain that connects the brain with the spinal cord and controls movement, sensation, and reflexes.
The part of the brain (in the frontal lobe of the left hemisphere) responsible for language comprehension and speech.
A bump of bone or tissue that forms at the big toe joint, causing inflammation and considerable pain.
A procedure used to divert the flow of blood or other fluids. When referring to the heart, shorthand for coronary artery bypass surgery, used to divert blood flow around a blocked coronary artery.
A mineral that the body needs for many vital functions, including bone formation, regulation of heart rate and blood pressure, and muscle contraction.
Hardened, thick skin that forms after repeated friction; often found on hands and the bottom of feet.
A group of diseases in which abnormal cells grow in an uncontrolled way, sometimes forming tumors.
The body’s smallest blood vessels; they deliver oxygen and nutrients to tissues.
An chemical found in hot chili peppers that is used in some pain relief creams.
The sugars and starches in food that provide the body with most of its fuel. Carbohydrates are one of three primary nutrients along with fats and proteins.
An odorless, colorless gas that is toxic to humans and animals at high levels; it is produced by cars, furnaces, fireplaces, and other equipment powered by combustion.
Any substance that can cause cancer.
The process by which a normal cell becomes cancerous.
A cancerous tumor that develops in the tissue that lines the organs of the body (the epithelium).

The sudden cessation of contractions capable of circulating blood to the body and brain. Also called sudden cardiac arrest. Cardiac arrest usually occurs as a result of a rapid ventricular rhythm (ventricular tachycardia) or a chaotic one (ventricular fibrillation). Death occurs within minutes unless cardiopulmonary resuscitation and defibrillation are available.
The use of a machine (heart/lung machine) to circulate and oxygenate the blood while surgery is performed on the heart.
A pump used to oxygenate and circulate blood through the body while the heart is stopped during open-heart surgery.
A combination of chest compressions and mouth-to-mouth breathing that keep oxygenated blood circulating to the brain and tissues. Commonly known as CPR.
Compounds such as lycopene and beta carotene that give red, yellow, and orange color to certain plants.
A condition that occurs when the median nerve, which runs from the forearm through the hand, is compressed; symptoms include pain, tingling, and numbness, as well as hand weakness.
Stiff connective tissue that provides support to other tissues and cushions joints.
Sudden paralysis of some or all muscles brought on by laughter, anger, fright, or strong emotions; a hallmark of narcolepsy.
A clouding or fogging of the lens of the eye that may blur or tint vision.
A thin tube that is inserted into the body to provide or drain fluids, or to carry tiny surgical instruments and cameras in minimally invasive surgeries.
A positively charged ion; cations in the body include sodium, potassium, and magnesium.
A hole in the tooth caused by advanced decay.

aligned.ro: Unitate de anestezie și terapie intensivă
aligned.def_en: Abbreviation for coronary care unit, a ward in a hospital that provides specialized care and extensive monitoring for patients with heart problems.

A disease characterized by damage to the small intestine caused by an oversensitivity to gluten, a protein found in wheat, rye, and barley. Celiac disease can interfere with the proper absorption of nutrients from food.
The basic building block of all living organisms.
The end stage in the life of a cell when the cell can no longer divide.
The brain, brainstem, and spinal cord.
The part of the brain that controls coordinated movement.
A weakening and ballooning of the wall of an artery in the brain.
The part of the brain involved in all forms of conscious experience, including thought, language, and memory.
Bleeding in the brain caused by the rupture of a blood vessel; another term for hemorrhagic stroke.
The medical term for a stroke.

Abbreviation for chronic fatigue syndrome, a disorder of ongoing, severe tiredness that interferes with a person’s ability to function well, isn’t improved with rest, and isn’t caused by another illness.
A hormone that signals the gallbladder to contract, releasing bile, and causes the pancreas to release enzymes used in digestion.
A waxy, fat-like substance produced by the liver and found in all food from animal sources; an essential component of body cells and a precursor of bile acids and some hormones.
A thin layer of blood vessels and connective tissue between the white of the eye (sclera) and the retina.
A threadlike structure, found in the nucleus of each cell, that carries almost all of a cell’s genes.
A disorder of ongoing, severe tiredness that interferes with a person’s ability to function well, isn’t improved with rest, and isn’t caused by another illness.
Pain that persists after an injury has healed or a disease is over.
Long-term, severe pain that doesn’t spring from an injury or illness, that interferes with daily life, and is often accompanied by other problems, such as depression, irritability, and anxiety.
A fat globule that ferries triglyceride from the intestine to the liver and fat tissue.
Small, hairlike structures on the surface of some cells.
The body’s biological clock that regulates the sleep/wake cycle and other physiological processes.
A chronic disease of the liver that progressively destroys the liver’s ability to aid in digestion and detoxification.
Abbreviation for creatine kinase, an enzyme found in the heart, brain, and skeletal muscle. Levels of creatine kinase are tested to diagnose certain illnesses.
A study that tests a therapy in humans, rather than in laboratories or on animals.
Part of the ear that converts sound into electrical signals that the brain interprets as a particular sound.
A small electronic device that is implanted in the inner ear to restore some hearing to a deaf person.
A small organic molecule, often made from B vitamins, that helps enzymes function in the body.
A form of therapy that aimed at recognizing and changing negative thoughts and behaviors.
Problems with memory, language, thinking, or other brain functions, varying from mild to serious difficulty.
Severe abdominal pain caused by spasms in the intestines or in a portion of the kidneys.
A fibrous protein that is the main component of connective tissue in the body.
The large intestine; a muscular tube that is 5 to 6 feet long. It compacts and moves solid waste.
A procedure to see inside the colon, using a long, lighted flexible tube mounted with a tiny camera.
Deep unconsciousness where the person is alive but unable to move or respond.
Any disease caused by bacteria, viruses, or other pathogens that is spread from person to person.
An imaging technique that uses a computer and x-rays passed through the body at different angles to create a detailed, nearly three-dimensional picture of the body.
The start of pregnancy, when an egg is fertilized by a sperm.
Cells in the retina that are sensitive to color and light.

An older term for heart failure, a disorder caused by a decrease in the heart’s ability to pump blood. Congestive heart failure referred specifically to the type of heart failure associated with the accumulation of excess fluid in the lungs or extremities.
Swelling or infection of the thin lining on the inside of the eyelid and the white part of the eyeball.
A group of tissues in the body that provide internal support and bind other tissues in the body, including bone, cartilage, tendons, and ligaments.
Shortening of a muscle, usually because of disease or lack of use, that limits joint movement.
A fluid injected into the bloodstream or swallowed so that organs will show up on x-rays.
A bruise. An injury that causes swelling, pain, and discoloration but doesn’t break the skin.
Rapid uncontrollable shaking of the body caused by muscles contracting and relaxing repeatedly.
An area of hardened, thickened skin usually caused by friction.
The clear dome that covers the front of the eye.

A condition in which one or more of the arteries feeding the heart become so narrow in spots that blood flow is impaired or stopped entirely, causing chest pain or a heart attack. Often called heart disease or coronary heart disease.
The middle layer and main structure of the hair shaft, consisting mainly of compact bundles of the protein keratin.
One of a class of stress hormones released during the fight-or-flight stress response.
Abbreviation for cardiopulmonary resuscitation, a combination of chest compressions and mouth-to-mouth breathing that keep oxygenated blood circulating to the brain and tissues.
A protein made by the liver. High amounts of C-reactive protein may indicate that arteries are clogged (atherosclerosis).
An enzyme that leaks into the bloodstream in high amounts if a muscle is damaged. Can be used to detect heart attack or muscle damage from other diseases.
A waste product created by muscle metabolism. Doctors sometimes test creatinine levels to examine kidney function.
A rare, untreatable, rapid form of dementia that is fatal.
A chronic disease that causes swelling of the digestive tract, pain, and diarrhea.
The part of the tooth that is visible above the gum line. Also a restoration that covers the crown of the tooth.
Use of extreme cold to freeze and destroy diseased tissue.
Abbreviation for C-reactive protein, a protein made by the liver. High amounts of C-reactive protein may indicate that arteries are clogged (atherosclerosis).
Part of the eye that changes shape so that the eye can focus on objects at different distances.
Computerized x-rays that provide detailed views of the body and brain. Also known as a computed tomography (CT) scan.
A disorder caused by high levels of the stress-hormone cortisol resulting in damage to the body, including abdominal obesity, rounded red face, and other symptoms.
A condition in which skin turns blue due to a lack of oxygen in the blood, often because of heart failure or lung disease.
An enzyme that helps blood cells known as platelets stick to each other, a key step in the formation of a blood clot.
Proteins in the body that act as messengers between immune system cells.
A mild and common condition that is characterized by an itchy, flaky scalp and that may extend to the ears, face, and chest. Also known as seborrheic dermatitis.
Type of medication used to relieve nasal congestion.
The delivery of an electric shock to the heart to stop an abnormal rhythm and restore a normal heartbeat.
Any disease in which the organs or tissues in the body are damaged progressively over time.
Sudden, severe confusion that occurs because of a mental or physical illness.
A false or irrational belief held by a person despite evidence to the contrary.
A loss of brain function that worsens over time and affects memory, thinking, behavior, and language.
Spidery-looking immune system cells that help protect the body from harmful substances.
A metal post inserted into the alveolar bone to support an artificial tooth or other prosthesis.
The substance found in the nucleus of cells that contains the genetic instructions for that living organism.
The middle layer of skin that contains most of the skin’s structures, like collagen, nerves, glands, and hair follicles.
A disease in which the body does not properly produce or use insulin, resulting in abnormally high levels of sugar (glucose) in the blood.
The dome-shaped sheet of muscle at the base of the lungs that helps move air in and out of the lungs.
The part of plant foods the body can’t digest or absorb. Also called roughage.
Vitamins, minerals, herbs, and other substances taken in hopes of improving health.
The series of hollow organs, including the mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine (colon), rectum, and anus, which break down and digest food and expel waste.
A form of the hormone testosterone that spurs the prostate gland to enlarge (benign prostatic hyperplasia).

A drug that eases the heart's workload and decreases the buildup of fluid in the lungs and other parts of the body by promoting the excretion of water and salts. Diuretics (also called water pills) are used to treat high blood pressure, heart failure, and some congenital heart defects.
The bulging out of small pouches or sacs of tissue from the colon wall.
An abbreviation for deoxyribonucleic acid, the substance in cells that contains the genetic instructions that direct their function.
A chemical messenger (neurotransmitter) that affects movement and thought processes.
Medication used to treat high blood pressure or an enlarged prostate gland.
The upper part of the small intestine.
A thin protective membrane covering the brain and spinal cord.

A speech disability caused by an injury to the brain centers controlling the face, mouth, neck, or throat. People with dysarthria may be able to understand speech and form the right words in their mind but cannot articulate them.
Painful sexual intercourse.
Difficulty chewing and swallowing food. Dysphagia is extremely common after a stroke.
Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath.
A disorder in which muscles twitch, causing uncontrollable twisting movements.
A thin membrane separating the ear canal and middle ear.
A substance that lubricates the inner ear and helps protect it from dirt, damage, and infections.
A diagnostic tool that uses high-frequency sound waves (ultrasound) to make images of the heart's size, structure and motion.
A serious condition related to high blood pressure that can threaten the life of a pregnant woman and her fetus.
Pregnancy in which a fertilized egg implants in an abnormal location outside the uterus, usually in the fallopian tubes. Ending the pregnancy is necessary.
A condition in which areas of the skin are dry, itchy, red, and cracked. Also known as atopic dermatitis.
Commonly used abbreviation for erectile dysfunction, the inability to get or maintain an erection sufficient for intercourse.
Swelling caused by abnormal accumulation of fluid in tissues.
Abbreviation for electroencephalogram, a test that measures the electrical activity of the brain and detects problems.
A sudden discharge of a fluid from a duct; often used to describe the expulsion of seminal fluid from the urethra of the penis during orgasm.
A flexible, stretchy protein found in skin and connective tissue.
A test that measures the electrical activity of the brain and detects problems.
A permanent hair removal technique that destroys follicles one at a time with a hair-thin needle inserted into the base of the follicle.
Minerals in the body that are electrically charged and play an important role in body processes, such as regulating fluid levels in the body. Examples include calcium and sodium.
A test that checks the health of muscles and the nerves that control them.
A chemical found in certain plants, such as raspberries and strawberries, that might help protect against cancer.

A type of stroke that occurs when a blood clot that has formed elsewhere in the body breaks off and travels through the bloodstream until it blocks an artery that normally supplies blood to the brain.
Any drug or other substance used to cause vomiting.
A severe and sometimes deadly inflammation of the brain that can be caused by a number of different viruses.
Continually present among people in a geographic region.
An inflammation of the heart lining or valves, usually caused by bacterial infection.
The inner layer of the wall of the heart.
Substances in the body that reduce pain and create a feeling of well-being.
Inserting a flexible tube equipped with a light and camera into the body to see inside a body cavity or organ.
Chemicals in the body that cause blood vessels to expand or relax, lowering blood pressure. Often referred to as EDRF.
Part of the nervous system that controls the gastrointestinal system.
A substance that speeds up another chemical reaction. For example, digestive enzymes help speed up the digestion of food.
White blood cells that play an important role in allergic reactions.
The occurrence of more cases of disease than expected within a population in a geographic area over a set period of time.
The outermost layer of skin.
A chemical that narrows blood vessels, increases heart rate, and helps trigger the fight-or-flight response to danger. Also called adrenaline.
A layer of cells which lines organs and structures in the body, protecting or enclosing them.
The inability to get or maintain an erection sufficient for intercourse. Sometimes referred to as ED.
Designing and arranging work objects so that the user is comfortable, efficient, and less likely to be injured.
The act of bringing up air from the stomach through the mouth with a characteristic sound. Commonly known as belching.
Redness of the skin because of widening of capillaries just below the surface of the skin.
A test involving red blood cells; used to check for different infections, inflammations, and cancers.
A hormone that controls red blood cell production.
Irritation and swelling of the esophagus.
The tube that carries food and liquids from the mouth to the stomach.
The main sex hormone in women.
A medication used to treat bone loss due to Paget's disease.
A tube connecting the middle ear and the back of the nose that lets air into the middle ear.
The component of thinking that organizes, plans, decides, and inhibits inappropriate impulses.
A structured program of physical activity that helps an individual become physically fit.
A protrusion or bulging of the eye that occurs with Graves’ eye disease. Tissues behind the eye swell, forcing the eyeball forward. Also called proptosis.
One of the three major nutrients, along with carbohydrates and proteins.
A lack of energy. A decrease over time in the ability to perform a physical or mental task.
Components of fats that can be used for energy by cells.
Feverish; having a high body temperature.
Thigh bone.
A substance found in plant foods that the body can’t digest.
Rapid and uncoordinated contractions of heart muscle fibers. When this occurs, the heart can't properly contract or pump blood.
A stringy protein that is the primary component of a blood clot.
A protein that helps stop bleeding by aiding in forming blood clots.
A cell that helps form the collagen and elastic fibers of connective tissue.
A condition causing pain and tender spots throughout the body.
The calf bone.
A medication for treating benign prostatic hyperplasia (enlargement of the prostate gland).
Excess gas in the stomach or intestines that is expelled from the anus.
Chemicals found in fruits, vegetables, wine, and tea that may protect cells from damage and have health benefits.
Tiny spots or lines that appear in a person’s field of vision when the jelly-like fluid of the eye breaks down with age. They are usually harmless, but can signal serious eye problems.
A mineral that protects teeth from decay and cavities.
A group of cells that form a small sac.
A hormone released by the pituitary gland that stimulates the production of eggs in women and sperm in men.
An unstable molecule in the body that plays a role in aging and can damage tissue; antioxidants help prevent free radical damage.
A simple sugar found in corn syrup, honey, and many sweet fruits.
Abbreviation for follicle-stimulating hormone, a hormone released by the pituitary gland that stimulates the production of eggs in women and sperm in men.
A chemical messenger in the brain that may help decrease anxiety and promote slow-wave sleep. Often referred to as GABA.
An abnormal but harmless mass of tissue, usually nerve cells.
Death of tissue in part of the body because blood has stopped flowing there.
Inflammation of the lining of the stomach.
A condition in which food and acid flow back into the esophagus from the stomach, causing heartburn.
The digestive tract.
Structures on chromosomes that are passed from parent to child. The basic unit of material that passes traits from parent to child.
Correction of a genetic defect by replacing an abnormal gene with a normal gene.
A copy of a brand-name drug whose patent has expired. These drugs are less expensive than brand-name drugs.
An antioxidant chemical found in certain plants, like soybeans.
Abbreviation for gastroesophageal reflux disease, a condition in which food and acid flow back into the esophagus from the stomach, causing heartburn.
Another term for gums: a form of oral tissue that covers the roots of teeth and surrounding bone.
Inflammation of the gums.
A condition in which the pressure inside the eye is too high, causing eye damage.
A hormone produced in the pancreas that raises blood sugar levels.
A simple sugar that is the body’s main source of energy.
The body’s fuel reserves. This substance, stored primarily in the liver and muscles, is later converted into glucose to provide cells with energy.
A form of arthritis that occurs when uric acid builds up in the joints; The big toe, knee, and ankle joints are most often affected.
A metric unit of weight equivalent to one-thousandth of a kilogram.
A broad range of reactions to bereavement, including sadness, tears, shock, confusion, and anger, among others.
The esophagus.
A form of oral tissue that covers the roots of teeth and surrounding bone. Also called the gingiva.
A perception of something that is not really there.
Feelings of contentment or joy; the overall experience of pleasure and meaning in life.
A disease in which the body’s immune system prevents the thyroid gland from producing enough thyroid hormone.

Abbreviation for hemoglobin A1c, the product formed by the attachment of glucose (blood sugar) to hemoglobin (a protein in red blood cells). A test for HbA1c is a useful measure of blood sugar control.

The common term for a myocardial infarction. It refers to the damage that occurs when blood flow to part of the heart is blocked or drastically restricted. The blockage usually stems from the rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque.
An extra or unusual sound heard during the heartbeat. A murmur may or may not be a sign of a problem in the heart.
The number of times the heart contracts in a minute, normally 60–100 times.
A burning pain in the chest or throat, caused when stomach acid backs up into the esophagus.
Bacteria that damages the lining the stomach. It is to blame for most ulcers and stomach inflammation. Often called H. pylori.
Cells that help fight disease by activating and directing other immune system cells.
Blood that leaks out of blood vessels and collects in the body.
Poor vision or blindness in half of the visual field, affecting one or both eyes.
The oxygen-carrying substance that gives red blood cells their color.
Coughing up or spitting up blood from the lungs.
Bleeding from a damaged blood vessel.
A type of stroke that occurs when a blood vessel leaks or bursts inside the brain, cutting off the supply of oxygen and nutrition to that part of the brain.
A drug that prevents blood from clotting.
Protection occurring when so many people in a region are immune to an infectious disease that it can’t spread to others.
A painful blistering skin rash caused by the chicken pox virus; also known as shingles.
When blood flowing through arteries pushes on artery walls with abnormally high force over a sustained period of time. Also called hypertension.
Part of the brain that plays an important role in processing long-term memories.
A substance released by the immune system when it is exposed to an allergen. Histamines cause many allergy symptoms.

Abbreviation for human immunodeficiency virus, the virus that leads to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). HIV damages immune cells so that they are no longer able to fight off other infections.
An itchy rash of usually short duration. Also known as urticaria.
The body’s ability to keep blood pressure, temperature, water levels, oxygen levels, and more set at the right levels for cells to survive.
An amino acid formed as part of the normal breakdown of protein.
Powerful chemicals that affect many processes in the body, including sexual function, mood, and growth.
Usually abbreviated as HIV, the virus that leads to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). HIV damages immune cells so that they are no longer able to fight off other infections.
A protein found on the surface of white blood cells that helps the body recognize and fight foreign substances.
An inherited disorder characterized by involuntary jerky movements and dementia.
A hydrating sugar secreted by cells.
The addition of hydrogen to a compound. Hydrogenation is used to solidify liquid vegetable oils. The process creates trans fats, which are harmful to the heart and blood vessels.
A hard substance that is a major component of bones and teeth.
An abnormally high amount of sugar in the blood.
Difficulty seeing objects that are nearby; farsightedness.
Increased production of cells in a normal tissue or organ; may be harmless or a sign of precancerous changes.

The medical term for high blood pressure. Hypertension is a major risk factor for stroke, especially hemorrhagic and lacunar strokes, because it puts excess stress on the walls of blood vessels and damages their delicate inner lining.
An agent that promotes and aids sleep.
A condition in which blood sugar drops to an abnormally low level.
A mild form of mania, in which a person has lots of energy, talks faster than normal, has racing thoughts, and elevated mood.
The medical term for low blood pressure.
A small area in the brain that produces hormones that control body temperature, hunger, moods, the stress response, and other key functions.
When all or part of the body doesn’t get enough oxygen.
An operation to remove a woman’s uterus.
Abbreviation for inflammatory bowel disease, a general term for two disorders—ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease—that cause the intestines to become swollen and inflamed.

aligned.ro: Clasificarea statistică internațională a bolilor și a problemelor de sănătate înrudite
aligned.ru: Международная статистическая классификация болезней и проблем, связанных со здоровьем
aligned.def_en: Abbreviation for implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device implanted in the chest and connected to the heart that delivers a shock to stop a potentially deadly rhythm and restore a normal (sinus) rhythm.
A condition or disease of unknown origin.
The final section of the small intestine.
The body’s ability to resist infection and disease.
Injection of harmless bacteria or viruses to spur the body to produce antibodies so it can resist a particular disease.
Treating disease by enhancing or suppressing the body’s immune system.
The inability of the penis to become firm or to stay firm enough to have sexual intercourse.
Involuntary passing of urine or feces.
The time between when a person is exposed to an infection and when symptoms appear.
The death of tissue due to a lack of blood.
The growth of harmful organisms that can cause disease, such as bacteria, in the body.
Arthritis caused by harmful organisms such as bacteria.
The large vein that carries blood from the lower half of the body to the heart.
The body’s reaction to injury or infection. It is characterized by swelling, heat, redness, and pain.
A general term for two disorders, ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, that cause the intestines to become swollen and inflamed. Often referred to as IBD.
Inserting fluids, such as medications, into the body by means of a hollow needle and syringe.
The body’s basic defenses against disease or infection that are present from birth.
The deepest part of the ear, consisting of the cochlea and the labyrinth.
The inability to fall asleep or remain asleep long enough to feel rested.
A hormone made by the pancreas that controls the amount of glucose (sugar) in the blood.
A condition in which the body produces insulin but can’t use it properly. This leads to diabetes.
Proteins made by the body to protect against viruses, bacteria, and other harmful agents.
A planned, often group, meeting with a person with addiction, with the aim of overcoming denial and inducing the individual to seek treatment.
One of the small, shock-absorbing cushions located between the vertebrae of the spine.
A hemorrhagic stroke caused by the rupture of a blood vessel and subsequent bleeding into the brain tissue.
A small artificial lens permanently fixed inside the eye to replace the natural lens during cataract surgery.
Salt compounds containing iodine that are used to control severe hyperthyroidism in special circumstances. They work by decreasing the thyroid gland’s production and secretion of thyroid hormone.
The colored ring in front of the lens that controls the size of the pupil and how much light enters the eye.
Inadequate blood supply to an organ or part of the body.
Clusters of hormone-producing cells, including alpha and beta cells, that appear throughout the pancreas.
The section of the small intestine between the duodenum and the ileum.
A junction in the body where bones are linked together.
A protein and the major component of the cuticle and cortex layers of hair; the same protein is found in nails, feathers, claws, and hooves.
Persistent dryness of the eye.
Substances produced when the body burns fat for energy or when the body doesn’t have enough insulin.
The final stage of chronic kidney disease. At this point, the kidneys can no longer eliminate waste products from the body.
An enzyme that breaks down milk sugar (lactose) in the body.
A rare but potentially lethal condition in which blood lactic acid levels increase.
The inability of the body to easily digest lactose, a sugar found in milk and dairy products.
A surgical procedure carried out with tiny instruments inserted through small openings in the skin.
A concentrated beam of light; lasers are used in certain surgeries and other medical procedures.
A drug or substance that induces bowel movements or makes the stool softer and looser.
Abbreviation for low-density lipoprotein. This so-called bad cholesterol can build up on artery walls, narrowing the artery and making a heart attack or stroke more likely.
A hormone produced by fat cells that acts on the brain to suppress appetite and burn stored fat.
An infected, diseased, or wounded area of tissue.
Chemicals that cause airways to swell when an allergic reaction occurs or in diseases like asthma.
A man-made version of the thyroid hormone thyroxine.
Abbreviation for luteinizing hormone, a hormone that controls ovulation in women. In men, luteinizing hormone triggers production of testosterone.
Sexual desire.
A blood-sucking parasite known as Pediculus humanus capitis that can cause an itchy scalp; infestations are highly contagious and especially common in school-age children.
A band of tissue that connects bones.
Antioxidant chemicals found in seeds like flax and sesame, as well as some fruits, vegetables, and grains.
A group of structures in the brain that help control memory, emotions, sexual arousal, and motivation.
A man-made version of the thyroid hormone triiodothyronine.
An enzyme secreted by the pancreas that helps the body break down fats.
Fats, oils, and waxes that serve as building blocks for cells or as energy sources. Lipids are also capable of accumulating in the artery walls to form plaque.
A combination of fat (lipid) and protein molecules bound together as packages. The combination allows fats and cholesterol to move easily through the blood.
A vital organ that removes waste products from the body and helps with digestion.
So-called bad cholesterol. If there is too much LDL in the blood, it can collect on artery walls, narrowing them and making heart attacks and strokes more likely.
A procedure in which a hollow needle is inserted into the lower part of the spinal canal to withdraw fluid for testing. Also called a spinal tap.
A natural substance found in green leafy vegetables.
A hormone that controls ovulation in women. In men, luteinizing hormone triggers production of testosterone.
An infectious disease transmitted by a tick bite.
Small, bean-shaped organs that filter germs and foreign matter out of the body. Also called lymph glands.
A system of channels that drains excess clear fluid, called lymph, from tissues and returns it into the bloodstream.
A type of white blood cell that can recognize foreign substances in the body.
A type of cancer that affects cells in the lymphatic system.
A type of white blood cell that destroys cell debris, bacteria, and foreign agents.

A scan that creates detailed pictures of internal organs; commonly referred to as MRI. Magnetic resonance imaging uses radio waves, a strong magnetic field, and a computer to produce images of organs and internal tissues.

Depression that interferes with daily life for an extended period. Episodes of major depression during bereavement can be distinguished from normal sadness by such symptoms as persistent feelings of worthlessness, thoughts about death, feelings of guilt, persistent trouble functioning, and marked mental and physical sluggishness.
Failure to eat or to properly absorb the nutrients needed for good health.
Sexual self-stimulation.
A government program that offers health care for low-income Americans of any age.
A government program that offers health care for Americans ages 65 and older.
Refers to the middle of something.
A substance that gives the skin, hair, and eyes their natural color.
The most dangerous type of skin cancer.
A hormone that regulates the body’s sleep-wake cycle.
A thin layer of tissue that surrounds or lines organs or cavities.
The three membranes that cover and protect the brain and spinal cord.
Swelling of the membranes that cover and protect the brain and spinal cord.
The point marking the end of menstruation, officially designated as one year after a woman’s final period.
The chemical reactions that occur in all living organisms to maintain life. An example is converting food into energy that the body needs to function.
The spread of cancer cells from the primary site to another part of the body.
Bacteria in the gut that help with the digestion of complex sugars.
Emptying the bladder. Also called urination or voiding.
The air-filled cavity behind the eardrum that contains the three small bones that transmit sound vibrations to the inner ear.
A metric unit of weight equivalent to one-thousandth of a gram. Abbreviated as mg.
A practice with its roots in Buddhism that encourages people to be more fully aware of the present moment. Often achieved through meditation.
Small structures within cells that create break down nutrients and create energy for cells. Known as the power producers or energy factories of cells.
An antibody is a protein molecule that can bind to a virus and mark it for destruction by the immune system. A monoclonal antibody is a man-made substance used to treat some viral and other diseases.
White blood cells that protect the body from disease by attacking and consuming foreign particles.
A thin layer that lines many cavities and structures in the body that are exposed to air in the environment, such as the nose, mouth, and lungs.
Abbreviation for medicated urethral system for erection. In this therapy, a small drug pellet is inserted into the tip of the penis to produce an erection.
The process by which a change occurs in genetic material and is inherited by the next generation.
Pain or tenderness in a muscle.
An abnormal weakness in a muscle or group of muscles.
Medical term for heart attack, the sudden death of part of the heart muscle from lack of oxygen.
Inflammation of the heart muscle (myocardium).
The middle layer of heart tissue. The muscular myocardium is sandwiched between the outer layer (epicardium) and the inner layer (endocardium).
A muscle cell.
Long interlocking strands that make up muscle fibers.
Nearsightedness. An optical error in which light rays meet and focus before reaching the retina, making objects that are far away appear blurry.
A protein that helps muscle contract and relax.
A sleep disorder that causes extreme sleepiness and uncontrollable sleep attacks, making a person fall asleep at inappropriate times during the day.
A type of white blood cell of the immune system. These cells destroy other cells that fail to display the right chemical flags signaling that they are normal cells.
The premature death of living cells or tissues.
Relating to an infant younger than 4 weeks of age.
An abnormal growth of tissue, either cancerous or benign.
Inflammation of the kidneys.
Kidney disease.
A physician trained to diagnose and treat disorders of the nervous system, including the brain and spinal cord.
A nerve cell.
Nerve damage and resulting loss of sensation, movement, or other function.
White blood cells that seek out and engulf foreign cells.

A compound produced by the endothelium (the lining of the interior walls of arteries) that helps widen blood vessels and counteract high blood pressure. Also called endothelium-derived relaxing factor.
A drug that relaxes blood vessels and increases the supply of blood and oxygen to the heart while reducing its workload. It is commonly used to treat angina.

Abbreviation for natural killer cells, a type of white blood cell of the immune system. These cells destroy other cells that fail to display the right chemical flags signaling that they are normal cells.
Waking up more than once during the night to urinate.
A chart or graph of mathematical calculations of risk; used in making treatment recommendations and predicting outcomes.
A drug that reduces swelling and pain.
A hormone produced by adrenal glands that puts the body on heightened alert when a threat is perceived (the fight-or-flight response). Also known as norepinephrine.
A hormone produced by adrenal glands that puts the body on heightened alert when a threat is perceived (the fight-or-flight response). Also known as noradrenaline.
Abbreviation for nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug, a drug that reduce swelling and pain.
Substances in foods that the body needs to survive.
Something not visible to the naked eye but seen under a microscope or through lab tests.
Beneficial fats, also known as n-3 fatty acids. These are polyunsaturated fat found in fatty fish, such as salmon.
A physician who deals with the diagnosis and treatment of cancer. There are three types—medical oncologists, radiation oncologists, and surgical oncologists.
Toenail fungus.
A physician who specializes in treating the eye and eye disease.
Any narcotic, natural or synthetic, that behaves in the body like an opium-derived drug.
A cable of specialized nerve fibers that transmit visual impulses from the eye to the brain.
A technician who helps select and fit eyeglasses or contact lenses for people with vision problems.
A characteristic frame of mind that leads a person to expect positive outcomes and to view the world as a positive place.
A health care professional licensed to examine the eye, and diagnose and treat some eye diseases.
A test to check for diabetes. It involves fasting overnight and having blood sugar levels checked before and after drinking a sugary solution.
The bony socket that holds the eyeball.
Surgery to remove the testicles. Usually done to remove a cancerous testicle or to lower testosterone levels and slow or halt the growth of prostate cancer.
The series of pleasurable, rhythmic muscle contractions that mark the peak of sexual arousal and the release of muscle tension.
The process by which bone is formed.
A joint disease in which the cartilage that lines the joints slowly deteriorates. Also called degenerative joint disease.
Cells that build bone tissue.
Cells that remove bone tissue.
A cell that is embedded in fully formed bone.
A bone infection caused by bacteria or fungi.
Mild thinning and weakening of the bones; bone density is lower than normal but not low enough to be classified as osteoporosis.
Significant thinning and weakening of bones over time, making them vulnerable to breaks.
An infection of the middle ear.
An abnormal bony growth in the middle ear that causes hearing loss.
Synonymous with epidemic. Sometimes used to refer to a local epidemic as compared to a larger, general epidemic.
The external part of the ear, as well as the external ear canal and the eardrum.
An unstable molecule in the body that plays a role in aging and can damage tissue. Also known as a free radical.
Abbreviation for peripheral artery disease, a condition caused by atherosclerosis in the arteries in the legs or leading to them.
The tissues that make up the roof of the mouth.
Treatment that relieves the symptoms of a serious illness, but does not cure the disease itself.
Sensation that the heart is beating rapidly or irregularly.
A gland in the abdomen that produces digestive enzymes and hormones.
A disease outbreak affecting large populations or a whole region, country, or continent.
Part of the nervous system that calms body systems excited by the stress hormones.
A hormone that controls levels of calcium and phosphorous in the blood and influences bone loss and growth.
Part of the brain. It plays a role in sensory processes, like pain and touch, and language.
A brain disorder that causes movement problems, including shaking, difficulty walking, and rigidity in muscles.
The thick bone that protects the knee joint; also known as the kneecap.
The underlying abnormalities that contribute to or are characteristic of a disease.

Abbreviation for polycystic ovary syndrome, an inherited disorder characterized by the formation of abnormal cysts in enlarged ovaries; a leading cause of female infertility and a common cause of excess facial or body hair (hirsutism).
A rare disease brought on by severe niacin deficiency that causes diarrhea, dermatitis, and dementia.
A raw, crater-like sore in the lining of the stomach or duodenum that causes burning stomach pain.
Passage of a fluid through a specific organ or an area of the body.
Inflammation of the pericardium, the heart's sac-like covering.
The fibrous sac that surrounds the heart and the roots of the major blood vessels.
The area of skin between the vagina and anus in women, and between the scrotum and anus in men.
An advanced stage of gum disease that attacks the teeth’s supporting structures.
A condition caused by atherosclerosis in the arteries in the legs or leading to them.
The parts of the nervous system outside of the brain, brain stem, and spinal cord.
Damage to the long nerves radiating from the spine to the arms and legs.
Wavelike movement of intestinal muscles that propels food through the digestive tract.
Inflammation of the membrane that line the abdominal cavity and surrounds most abdominal organs.
A form of anemia in which red blood cells enlarge and decrease in size due to an inability to properly absorb vitamin B12.
A characteristic frame of mind that leads a person to expect negative outcomes and to view the world as a negative or fearful place.
Pinpoint-sized red or purple spots that appear in clusters on the skin, caused by bleeding under the skin.
Abbreviation for positron emission tomography, a medical imaging test that uses a radioactive substance to assess organ and tissue function in the body and to look for disease.
Cells that can ingest other cells, bacteria, and foreign particles.
A medical treatment that uses a light source to activate a photosensitizing drug (one that becomes activated by light exposure). Often used in oncology, dermatology, and cosmetic surgery.
Sensitivity to light, often experienced during a migraine attack.

A physician who specializes in physical medicine, pain, and rehabilitation. These doctors diagnose and treat sports injuries and degenerative conditions like arthritis or low back pain, and oversee rehab for patients with severe impairments resulting from trauma, stroke, and other conditions.
A state of being physically sound and healthy; having the ability to perform physical activity well.
Substances made by plants that have biological effects in the human body. Examples include isoflavones, lycopene, lutein, and zeaxanthin.
A plant component that mimics the effects of estrogen hormones in the body.
A gland located in the middle of the brain, between the brain’s two hemispheres, that produces melatonin in response to declining light.
The so-called master gland, located at the base of the brain. It controls and regulates the thyroid and other glands throughout the endocrine system.
A false or inactive medication or treatment that may still offer relief despite being ineffective. In clinical trials, the effectiveness of a new drug is often tested against a placebo.
An inflammation of the plantar fascia; the leading cause of heel pain.
1) A layer of bacteria that forms on the surface of a tooth and can cause dental disease. 2) A fatty deposit in or on the walls of an artery, as part of atherosclerosis.
The fluid in which blood cells are suspended.
White blood cells that produce large quantities of antibodies as part of an immune system response.
An enzyme that breaks down the protein involved in clotting blood (fibrin), dissolving the clot.
A colorless, disk-shaped cell in the blood that is necessary for clotting.
An inherited disorder characterized by the formation of abnormal cysts in enlarged ovaries; a leading cause of female infertility and a common cause of hirsutism.
Excessive thirst.
An abnormal, noncancerous growth that protrudes from mucous membranes, like those found in the sinuses and colon lining.
Excessive urination.
A branch of psychology that studies mental health rather than illness, focusing on how life can be more happy and fulfilling.
A medical imaging test that uses a radioactive substance to assess organ and tissue function in the body and to look for disease. Commonly called a PET scan.
Nerve pain caused by the herpes zoster virus, also known as shingles.

A prolonged reaction to a traumatic event. Post-traumatic stress disorder can cause crippling anxiety and leading to other problems, such as sleep disturbances, depression, and substance abuse. Often referred to as PTSD.
Force times speed of movement. It reflects how quickly a given force is exerted.
A member of a class of drugs called alpha blockers. Prazosin eases the symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia by relaxing smooth muscle tissue in the capsule that surrounds the prostate.
High blood pressure during pregnancy accompanied by such signs as protein in the urine and swelling of the hands and feet; can progress to eclampsia, characterized by seizures.
Ejaculation that occurs before or immediately after penetration; this can interfere with a couple having a mutually satisfying sexual experience.
An erection that lasts longer than three hours. Emergency medical treatment is required to prevent permanent damage to the penis.
The smallest known infectious agent; unlike a virus or bacterium it is made entirely of protein and contains no nucleic acid or chromosomes.
Live microorganisms used to benefit health, such as the L. acidophilus bacteria found in yogurt.
A female steroid hormone produced by the ovaries that prepares the uterine lining for pregnancy.
A condition in which an organ or other body part drops from its normal position.
The ability to sense the position of one’s body in space, in relation to other objects.
Forward bulging or displacement of an organ, especially of an eye. See exophthalmos.
A group of chemicals that have hormone-like actions; prostaglandins help regulate blood pressure and contraction of smooth-muscle cells (for example, those in the lining of the blood vessels).
Cancer of the prostate gland.
A walnut-shaped gland at the base of the male bladder. It produces a fluid that forms part of semen.
An inflammation of the prostate gland, sometimes caused by a bacterial infection, which may result in painful or difficult urination.
An artificial device such as a hearing aid, artificial joint, or dentures that substitutes for a missing body part.

One of the three major nutrients (along with carbohydrates and fats). It is used by the body for building and repairing tissues. Protein is derived primarily from animal sources but can be obtained from nuts and seed, some grains, and other plant sources.
Itching.
Abbreviation for prostate-specific antigen, a protein produced by the prostate. Elevated levels may indicate the presence of cancer, benign prostatic hyperplasia, or prostatitis.
A common skin disease characterized by thickened patches of inflamed red skin; sometimes accompanied by painful joint swelling and stiffness.
A form of therapy that focuses on how life events, desires, and close relationships lead to conflict, symptoms such as anxiety or depression, and difficulty in managing life’s tasks.

Abbreviation for post-traumatic stress disorder, a prolonged reaction to a traumatic event. PTSD can cause crippling anxiety and leading to other problems, such as sleep disturbances, depression, and substance abuse.
The nerve that carries sensation from the genital area to the central nervous system.
A condition caused by excess fluid accumulating in the lungs, making breathing difficult.
Blockage of one or more arteries in the lungs by a blood clot that formed elsewhere, often in the legs. Typically accompanied by sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, and cough.
The veins that carry blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
The difference between systolic blood pressure and diastolic blood pressure (systolic pressure minus diastolic pressure = pulse pressure). Pulse pressure may help predict heart disease risk.
The dark, circular opening in the middle of the iris of the eye.
A thick, yellow or green liquid that is composed of dead cells and bacteria, most often found at the site of a bacterial infection.
A form of vitamin B6.
A period of time in which a sick person is kept away from others to prevent the spread of disease.
Energy in the form of particles or waves, such as x-rays and gamma rays. Radiation is often used to help make a diagnosis, as in x-rays, or as a treatment for cancer.
A period of intense brain activity during sleep, often associated with dreams; named for the rapid eye movements that occur during this time. Also called dreaming sleep.
The last 12 centimeters of the colon, through which waste is eliminated from the body.
Abbreviation for rapid eye movement, which occurs during a period of sleep characterized by intense brain activity, often associated with dreams.
An enzyme released by the kidney that stimulates production of angiotensin and aldosterone, two substances in the body that affect blood pressure.

The process by which gases enter the body, including external respiration (breathing), and internal respiration, in which oxygen taken in by the lungs is carried by the blood to tissues and carbon dioxide is removed.
Achy or unpleasant feelings in the legs associated with a need to move. Most prominent at night, making it hard to fall asleep or stay asleep.
The process of reviving a person who is not breathing or whose heart is not beating using techniques such as artificial respiration and heart massage.
The innermost layer of the eye, which converts light energy to electrical energy and sends visual images to the brain via the optic nerve.
Any one of over 100 disorders that cause inflammation in connective tissues.
Pain and stiffness of soft tissues in and around joints.
An inflammatory autoimmune disease that typically attacks the connective tissue of the joints, causing them to become painful, inflamed, and sometimes deformed.

The branch of medicine devoted to the study and treatment of diseases marked by inflammation, degeneration, or metabolic problems of the connective tissues (particularly the joints and related structures).
Reshaping the cartilage and bone of the nose to achieve the desired profile. Commonly known as a nose job.
Any factor that can cause a person to be more likely to develop a disease. For example, smoking is a risk factor for lung cancer.
Abbreviation for restless legs syndrome, an achy or unpleasant feelings in the legs associated with a need to move. Most prominent at night, making it hard to fall asleep or stay asleep.
The portion of the tooth below the gum line.
A group of tendons and muscles used to raise the arm from the side and rotating the shoulder.
The larger triangular bone at the base of the spine.
Abbreviation for seasonal affective disorder, sadness and depression brought on by a lack of exposure to sunlight. SAD usually appears in the fall or winter and subsides in the spring.
A watery solution that contains a small amount of salt and is often used to administer drugs or as a substitute for plasma.
One of three pairs of glands that pour lubricating fluids and digestive enzymes into the mouth.
A cancer that arises in the soft tissues of the body that connect, support, and separate other tissues or organs. Sarcomas can occur almost anywhere in the body.
A circular drainage system in the eye located where the clear cornea, white sclera, and colored iris meet to form an angle.
Pain along the course of the sciatic nerve (which runs from the buttock, down the back and side of the leg, and into the foot and toes), often because of a herniated disk.
The white of the eye; a tough, protective coating of collagen and elastic tissue that, with the cornea, makes up the outer layer of the eyeball.
An autoimmune disease in which the skin thickens and hardens; sometimes other parts of the body are affected, and joint pain may result.
An abnormal lateral, or sideways, curvature of the spine.
A disease caused by vitamin C deficiency, characterized by bruising, poor wound healing, bleeding of the gums, and loosened teeth.
A gland that opens into a terminal hair follicle; it secretes sebum, the natural oily conditioner of hair.
A mild and common condition that is characterized by an itchy, flaky scalp and that may extend to the ears, face, and chest. Also known as dandruff.
The release of chemical substances produced by the body; or the substance that is produced.
Shorthand for erythrocyte sedimentation rate—a test involving red blood cells used to check for different infections, inflammations, and cancers.
A drug or a procedure that has a calming effect and relieves anxiety and tension.
A sudden, involuntary contraction of muscles that results in rhythmic contortions of the body, often accompanied by a loss of consciousness. Also called a convulsion.
Gradual loss of body functions caused by the biological aging process, which increases risk of disease, disability, and death.
The destruction or infection of tissues by disease-causing organisms, usually accompanied by a fever.
A condition in which disease-causing organisms have spread to the bloodstream from an infection elsewhere in the body. Also known as blood poisoning.
A neurotransmitter that helps regulate sleep and appetite, mediate moods, and inhibit pain.
A problem with any area of a person’s sexual response that causes distress.

A serious medical condition in which there too little blood flows to the outer portions of the body, resulting in cold, sweaty skin; a weak pulse; irregular breathing; and dilated pupils. Shock can be caused by a loss of blood, severe heart problems, severe infections, allergic reactions, or drug overdoses.
Information the brain stores temporarily, from milliseconds to minutes.
An unwanted, and sometimes dangerous, reaction caused by medication or other treatment.
Section of the colon leading to the rectum that makes an S-shaped curve.

Temporary pause in breathing during sleep, lasting at least 10 seconds and associated with a fall in blood oxygen or arousal from sleep. Obstructive sleep apnea is caused by an obstruction in the airway blocking air flow; central sleep apnea occurs when the brain temporarily stops sending signals to the muscles that control breathing.
A feeling of paralysis that may occur during the transition between wakefulness and sleep if the REM sleep stage begins before a person is fully asleep; classically associated with narcolepsy.
A section of the digestive system that includes the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum and plays the major role in absorbing nutrients for the body.
Sleepwalking.
An involuntary muscle contraction.
A ring of muscle that surrounds an opening and can be contracted to close the opening. For example, the muscles found at the anus and the opening of the bladder are sphincters.
A congenital defect in which part of the spinal column fails to develop completely, leaving part of the spinal cord exposed.
A narrowing of the spinal canal, which can result in compression of nerve roots.
Use of a hollow needle to withdraw fluid from the lower part of the spinal canal for testing. Also called a lumbar puncture.

A simple, painless breathing test performed in a physician’s office or pulmonary function laboratory that measures how fast air can be forced from the lungs and the total amount of air that can be emptied from the lungs.
A painful spasm in the left upper abdomen below the rib cage, produced by areas of trapped gas in the colon.
A general term for degeneration of the spine that causes narrowing of the spinal canal and the small openings (intervertebral foramina) through which spinal nerves exit the canal.
A stretched or torn ligament.
A mixture of saliva and mucus that is coughed up from the respiratory tract. Sputum may be examined in a laboratory for signs of disease.
An abnormal narrowing of a passageway, such as a blood vessel, or other type of opening in the body.
A wire mesh device inserted into an artery to prop it open once a blockage has been cleared by angioplasty.

1) A surgical procedure or other method that results in a person being unable to reproduce. 2) The process by which materials are thoroughly cleaned of all organisms that could cause disease or infection.
Another term for corticosteroids—steroid medications made to mimic hormones produced naturally by the adrenal glands. They are used to treat a wide range of health problems.
A substance that speeds up chemical reactions inside cells and provides a boost of energy. Examples include caffeine and amphetamine.
The sac-like organ of the digestive system between the esophagus and the duodenum which breaks down food and moves it along to the small intestine to be digested.

An innate survival response in which certain hormones are released, increasing blood flow to the brain or heart. The stress response leads to an energy surge, enabling a person to flee dangerous situations. Ongoing stress, however, can sap energy and damage health.
Blockage or rupture of a blood vessel supplying the brain; often leads to impaired brain function or death.
Deepest layer of skin, which consists of connective tissue and fat.
A blood clot in the brain between the cerebral cortex and the dura.
Continued substance use despite substance-related social or interpersonal problems.

A condition characterized by excessive and often compulsive substance use, impaired control over substance use, continued use of substances despite adverse consequences, and withdrawal symptoms that emerge when the substance use is discontinued.
The major vein that carries deoxygenated blood from the upper body to the heart.
A solid form of medication that is inserted in the rectum or vagina and absorbed into the bloodstream.
An offshoot of the autonomic nervous system; it sends signals to prepare the body for action when stress hormones are released in response to perceived or real dangers.
The junction between two neurons, across which chemical neurotransmitters carry messages.
Fainting or loss of consciousness caused by a temporary shortage of oxygen in the brain.
A thin membrane that lines joint capsules and produces synovial fluid.
A connective tissue disease that can affect internal organs, nervous system, skin, and joints.
The brief period during which the heart contracts during a normal heartbeat, pumping blood into the aorta and the pulmonary artery.
Abbreviation for T lymphocyte, a type of white blood cell that is produced in the bone marrow and is part of the body’s immune system.
A type of white blood cell that is produced in the bone marrow and is part of the body’s immune system. Also called a T cell.
An abnormally fast heartbeat, usually above 100 beats per minute.
A drug used by women to prevent breast cancer or its recurrence.
A hardened layer of plaque that builds up on teeth. Also called calculus.
One of the four major subdivisions of the two hemispheres of the brain’s cerebral cortex. The temporal lobe plays a role in hearing, long-term memory, and behavior.
A cord of collagen fibers that connect a muscle to a bone.
A male hormone that stimulates bone and muscle growth and sexual development in men; also produced in lesser amounts in women, promoting sex drive and muscle growth.
A brain structure that relays sensory information to other parts of the brain; also plays a role in memory consolidation.
A class of oral medication that improves sensitivity to insulin.
Breaking up a blood clot.
Formation of a blood clot (called a thrombus) in a blood vessel or chamber of the heart.
A specialized organ of the immune system located in the upper-middle chest where T cells mature.
A two-lobed gland located in the front of the neck below the larynx (voice box). It secretes hormones that help regulate the body's metabolism and calcium balance.
Two iodine-containing hormones called thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). They help regulate the body's metabolism and calcium balance.
One of two types of major thyroid hormone manufactured by the thyroid gland. It contains four iodine atoms. Also known as T4.
Abbreviation for transient ischemic attack, a brain attack that resolves on its own within 24 hours. Sometimes called a mini-stroke, a TIA is often an early warning sign of an impending stroke.
The large bone of the calf, or shinbone.
An herbal product made by soaking an herb or other plant material in a mixture of water and alcohol to extract certain ingredients believed to be medicinal or beneficial.
Athlete’s foot.
A ringing in the ears or some other sound that has no external cause.
A group of cells that are specialized to do a certain job and are joined together to form a body structure, such as muscle or kidney.
Infectious disease that attacks the teeth. Also called dental caries.
A poison, usually one produced by a living organism.

Abbreviation for tissue plasminogen activator, a clot-dissolving enzyme produced naturally in the blood vessels and artificially produced as a medication. tPA is used to break down blood clots in the treatment of heart attack, ischemic stroke, and pulmonary embolism. tPA must be used within a few hours after symptoms begin.

A type of fat made during hydrogenation of liquid vegetable oil. Trans fats are found in many solid margarines, commercially prepared baked goods, and fried foods in many restaurants. Trans fats increase harmful low-density lipoprotein, decrease protective high-density lipoprotein, and promote blood clotting and inflammation. Also known as trans fat.
A brain attack that resolves on its own within 24 hours. Sometimes called a mini-stroke or TIA, a transient ischemic attack is often an early warning sign of an impending stroke.
The process of removing an organ or other donated body part from one person and implanting it in another person.
A rhythmic, quivering movement of muscles that can be caused by diseases such as Parkinson disease, side effects of medication, or old age.
A three-flap valve that sits between the right atrium and the right ventricle.

A class of medications that relieve depression by interfering with the reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine by neurons in the brain and spinal cord. At low doses, they are effective as pain medicines.
